<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Cleo Fields>: H.R. 941 was opposed by all Committee Democratic Members because it would reduce transparency in the small business lending market by delaying and significantly narrowing the application of Section 1071 of Dodd-Frank's small business loan data collection requirements. The bill does this by only covering loans to small businesses with annual revenues of $1 million, instead of $5 million, as required by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) final rule. The bill would also exempt any lender that has less than $10 billion in assets or originates less than 2,500 small business loans annually in each of the past two years (instead of 100 loans in CFPB's rule or 500 loans in the original bill), significantly limiting the amount of lending data gathered and made available to the public. The bill would also extend compliance dates until June 2031, with an additional safe harbor preventing enforcement of non-compliance until June 2033, nearly a quarter of a century after Congress enacted this requirement into law. This approach will limit the CFPB rule's benefits of promoting competition, lowering borrowing costs for entrepreneurs, curbing discriminatory practices. A similar bill was included in a larger package last Congress, H.R. 8338 (118th), the Clarity in Lending Act, that all Committee Democratic Members similarly opposed.
In March 2023, the CFPB finalized a rule implementing Section 1071 of Dodd-Frank,\1\ to drive down costs for small businesses, especially women-owned, LGBTQ-owned businesses and businesses owned by people of color. CFPB's Section 1071 rule requires lenders to collect and report information about the small business credit applications they receive, including geographic and demographic data (that's self-reported by business owners on a voluntary basis), lending decisions, and the price of credit. The rule would work in tandem with the Community Reinvestment Act, which requires certain financial institutions to meet the needs of the communities they serve. The increased transparency benefits small businesses, family farms, financial institutions, and the broader economy.
\1\CFPB, Small business lending rulemaking (Accessed June 8, 2023).
Arguably, had CFPB's Section 1071 rulemaking been in place before the pandemic, policymakers would have been able to not only design relief programs that were better targeted, but also to better monitor which small businesses received support and which were left out of programs like the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP). Industry studies also affirm how important fair lending rules are to the nation's economic vitality. For instance, one Citigroup study estimates that fair access to lending for Black-owned small businesses alone would have resulted in $650 billion in additional business revenue per year, as well as created an additional 6.1 million jobs per year.\2\ Moreover, the CFPB conducted a pilot study in 2024 where they found that Black-owned small businesses received disparate treatment compared to White-owned small businesses by the same bank, finding that Black participants received less encouragement to apply for a loan and were more likely to be steered into alternative credit products, like a home equity credit product where the owner's personal residence would be at risk if they default on the loan.\3\
\2\Citigroup, Closing the Racial Inequality Gaps: The Economic Cost of Black Inequality in the U.S. (Sep.2020).
\3\CFPB, CFPB Pilot Study Finds Differential Treatment in Small Business Lending Markets (Nov. 13, 2024).
Since its finalization, Section 1071 has come under attack in the courts and from Republicans. In May 2023, plaintiffs filed a lawsuit in a Texas federal district court challenging the validity of the rule and a motion seeking a preliminary injunction.\4\ Opponents of the rule have argued that the rulemaking would add burdensome new requirements on small lenders and reduce small business lending altogether. Yet, community lenders\5\ and small business advocates alike have underlined the importance of CFPB's small lending rules in creating a fairer and more transparent marketplace for lenders and small businesses. It is also likely that rules shining a light on small business lending will likely result in increased lending to underserved businesses, including farms, as was observed in the implementation of similar sunshine statutes like the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA). In fact, changes to HMDA data in 1990 and 1993 corresponded with a 70% increase in conventional home purchase lending to Black borrowers, and a 48% increase in lending to Latinx borrowers, from 1993 to 1995.\6\
\4\John L. Culhane, Jr., Richard J. Andreano, Jr. & Michael Gordon, Plaintiffs challenging Section 1071 final rule seek preliminary injunction; Ballard Spahr to hold June 15 webinar, Ballard Spahr (accessed Jun. 8, 2023).
\5\Accion Opportunity Fund, CEO Luz Urrutia's Congressional Testimony on Lending Transparency (Mar. 2023).
\6\NCRC, Home Loans to Minorities and Low- and Moderate-Income Borrowers Increase in the 1990s, but then Fall in 2001: A Review of National Data Trends from 1993 to 2001 (Apr. 2023).
CFPB set the current thresholds to ensure that only the largest small business lenders would have to comply, and exempted more than 80% of depository institutions from the rule, including most community banks and credit unions. The original bill proposes raising the minimum loan threshold from 100 to 500 annual originations for the prior two years, which is estimated to limit the obligation to only 4-5% of such lenders.\7\ However, the revised bill goes well above even that, raising the threshold to 2,500 loans annually for the past two years while also exempting financial institutions with less than $10 billion, even if they are major small business lenders.
\7\See Federal Register, CFPB--Small Business Lending Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B) (May 31, 2023).
Moreover, the thresholds in CFPB's current rule capture roughly 94% of the small business loan market by number of originations and 82% by loan amounts, helping ensure there is sufficient data to promote a fair and competitive marketplace. However, the bill would further limit the scope by lowering the small business revenue threshold to $1 million from $5 million, which would exclude several businesses that have faced challenges to accessing fair and affordable small business financing. And even though Trump's CFPB has already pushed back many of the compliance periods to 2028, while also recently advancing a much worse rule undermining the entire intent of Section 1071,\8\ this bill would mandate many of those bad reforms and extend the compliance deadline until June 1, 2031, and provide a new safe harbor that would prevent enforcement for non-compliance until June 1, 2033. Even though small business owners had to sue the CFPB to ensure Section 1071 would eventually be implemented, this proposal would significantly narrow the scope and timeliness of its implementation.
\8\See Federal Register, CFPB--Small Business Lending Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B) (May 1, 2026). (May 1, 2026); and CFPB, Small business lending rulemaking (accessed May 1, 2026). Also see NCRC, CFPB Section 1071 Final Rule A Massive Step Backward (Apr. 30, 2026).
More than 200 small business, civil rights, farm, community, consumer and other organizations, including Americans for Financial Reform, Center for Responsible Lending, HEAL (Health, Environment, Agriculture, Labor) Food Alliance, Main Street Alliance, and National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC).\9\
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 941.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Brad Sherman,
